reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / cerebrovascular headache literature
clinicalPearls: Hallmark is recurrent thunderclap headache, often over days to weeks, sometimes with focal deficits or seizures
Angiography shows multifocal segmental narrowing with a beaded appearance that resolves within about three months
Frequently precipitated by vasoactive drugs, cannabis, sympathomimetics, serotonergic agents, or the postpartum state
Complications include cortical subarachnoid haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke, and reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy
Cerebrospinal fluid is usually normal or near-normal, helping distinguish it from CNS vasculitis
Removal of triggers and calcium-channel blockers are the mainstays, with corticosteroids generally avoided
The reversibility of arterial narrowing on repeat imaging is central to confirming the diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is a transient disturbance of cerebral arterial tone in which dysregulation of vascular smooth muscle produces multifocal segmental vasoconstriction of medium and large cerebral arteries. The abnormal vasomotor control, often provoked by vasoactive substances, hormonal changes, or the postpartum state, causes waves of constriction and dilatation that account for the recurrent thunderclap headaches. Impaired perfusion can lead to ischaemic infarction, while vessel wall stress and reperfusion contribute to cortical subarachnoid haemorrhage and posterior reversible encephalopathy; the vasoconstriction characteristically resolves over weeks to a few months.
additionalDifferentials: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome from other causes
additionalInvestigations: CT or MR angiography demonstrating multifocal segmental narrowing, repeated to show reversibility
Non-contrast CT and MRI to detect cortical subarachnoid haemorrhage, infarction, or oedema
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis to help exclude vasculitis and subarachnoid haemorrhage
Review of medications and drug screen for vasoactive precipitants
Digital subtraction angiography in selected cases when non-invasive imaging is inconclusive
redFlags: Recurrent thunderclap headaches, which mandate exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage
New focal neurological deficit or seizure suggesting stroke or oedema
Persistent or worsening narrowing that raises concern for true vasculitis
reference.prognosis: Most patients recover fully within days to weeks as the vasoconstriction resolves, but a minority suffer permanent deficits from stroke or haemorrhage, and recurrence is uncommon but possible.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as CNS vasculitis and giving prolonged immunosuppression
Missing an underlying vasoactive drug or postpartum trigger
Failing to repeat vascular imaging to confirm reversibility
Using corticosteroids, which may worsen outcomes in this condition
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Remove and avoid precipitants, including vasoactive drugs, cannabis, sympathomimetics and serotonergic agents
Treat with a calcium-channel blocker such as nimodipine or verapamil to relieve headache and vasospasm
Avoid corticosteroids, which are associated with worse outcomes
Provide analgesia, rest and blood-pressure control during the symptomatic phase
Monitor for and manage complications including cortical subarachnoid haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke and posterior reversible encephalopathy
Repeat vascular imaging to confirm resolution of the vasoconstriction over the ensuing months
